Following Angela Davis’s schematic reading, one might argue that an understanding of freedom conceived from the perspective of the servant’s consciousness is already prefigured in Hegel’s account of domination and servitude. Identifying the truth of self-consciousness as the servant’s consciousness, after all, owes itself precisely to the experience of independence made possible for the servant through her own practice. But if read as part of a standpoint theory of normativity, it becomes clear how it is possible that a historically very specific and thus minority practice can have universal significance. The counter-communities of oppressed and marginalized groups, exemplified by the maroon communities, are able to form better political formations out of their liberation practices than the dominant groups whose institutions – the bourgeois state – correspond to the false concept of freedom developed out of a domination interest.
